articles.title: BBC appeals against decision to allow Trump's $10bn lawsuit to go ahead
articles.text:
The BBC has lodged an "urgent" appeal against a US judge's decision to allow Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the corporation to go ahead.

The US president is suing the BBC for defamation over the way an episode of Panorama edited a speech he gave in January 2021, shortly before the riot at the US Capitol.

Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that the defamation case could proceed after the BBC sought to dismiss it.

The BBC has now filed an appeal with a higher court, saying there is a "complete lack of evidence" that anyone in Florida accessed the programme, and that the broadcaster made "rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary" in the US.

A BBC spokesman said: "We are surprised and disappointed by the court's decision that this case should be heard in Florida.

"As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK - and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.

"Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling."

President Trump's lawsuit accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for the edit in Trump: A Second Chance, which it said had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

But the corporation argued that the Panorama episode, which was broadcast in 2024, did not meet the legal criteria for defamation.

Earlier this month, federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not rule on the merits of the case.

President Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a post on Truth Social at the time.

The BBC has now lodged an appeal with the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, arguing that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.

Trump has been ordered to answer questions under oath as part of the lawsuit by 22 January.

Judge Kuntz has scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

articles.title: Great British Bake Off winner crowned after high-stakes final
articles.text:
Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.

The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies.

Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.

He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.

"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.

"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."

Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends.

"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.

Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".

articles.title: Pete Edochie: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor dies aged 79
articles.text:
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.

Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.

"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.

The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.

Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.

He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

articles.title: Substance at Don Toliver Manchester show may be linked to robberies, police say
articles.text:
An "unknown substance" that prompted a mass evacuation at a rap concert may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue, police have said.

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One person was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert but no arrests had been made and the substance had not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public.

"We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.

In a statement on Tuesday evening, Co-op Live said it was conducting a "full review" into the incident.

"The safety and security of our guests, artists and staff remain our highest priority, and we take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The venue, which opened in 2024, apologised to fans for what should have been an "enjoyable evening" and said it expects no disruption to future events.

The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.

Many were advised to seal their clothes in a bag overnight.

articles.title: Blade Runner 2099: Hunter Schafer's series 'not just about AI'
articles.text:
"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.

The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.

While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.

At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.

The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.

It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.

Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.

"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.

"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."

Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.

Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.

The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans.

"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.

"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."

But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.

"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.

The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.

Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.

"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.

"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"

Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.

This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?

"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.

"It makes you want to learn more."

Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.

"I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says.

"They crave new kind of worlds and new things.

"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."

Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".

"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.

"Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

articles.title: London Museum: What's it like inside the new Smithfield Market venue?
articles.text:
Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?

Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.

"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.

The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.

And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.

"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.

A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.

Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry.

Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.

Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.

"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.

"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."

Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago, when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.

Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.

"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.

"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.

A wide staircase to one side descends into what is called Past Time.

Down here is what once was street level of Roman London, and curator Annette Day explains that "we felt that right in the guts, in the earth of the city, that was the place where we should explore London".

A weaving route beneath a seven-metre-high brick vaulted ceiling tells the capital's story.

It starts with the city's creation by the Romans and moves through medieval times and London's place as the centre of the British Empire, before ending with the 2012 Olympic Games, a time when "London looked at itself and the world looked at London", says Day.

Along the way are all manner of objects.

There's Charles I's execution vest, Queen Victoria's mourning dress, a white 1960s Ford Cortina, an overstuffed taxidermy cat called Oliver and the shimmering Elizabethan jewellery of the Cheapside Hoard.

Even with its planned events, shops and eateries, Ament says it is all these objects which remain "the essence of the museum" because they "tell stories in a compelling way".

She sees the museum as a shared space for everyone, somewhere for Londoners and tourists alike to connect with people and stories from the past and now.

"Think of this as like one of my favourite buses, the number 63 bus. You meet the world on it. And you meet the world in here."

Most important of all, she says, is that the London Museum must always represent and reflect the city it is in.

"The story of London is tough and joyful at the same time. That's why we use 'grit and glitter' as a tagline - it's both of those things, those dualities can exist. And we shouldn't be frightened of that history," she says.

"We are making a museum and it will never stop, just like London never stops. There's always cranes in London and there'll always be new things in London Museum."

articles.title: BBC and Netflix team up for new CBeebies hub on streamer
articles.text:
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.

Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.

The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.

BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.

CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.

Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.

BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.

"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.

Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".

She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."

articles.title: First Children's Booker prize reveals shortlist ' full of surprises' - and its child judges
articles.text:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.

Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.

The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.

Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.

He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.

"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.

Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."

Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.

"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".

Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".

"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."

He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.

"That's why we're here! To fight the fight. To make sure our children have as many opportunities as possible to discover how pleasurable, how bonding, how thrilling and enriching and fortifying it can be to slip out of the prison of the present into the infinity of the story."

Ibrahim told me "my friends don't read books at all".

He doesn't try to persuade them. "I let them live their life. I live my life".

But if he were to try to, what would he say?

"Put a timer on your phone, make sure it's blocked and then they'll decide to do something more productive. I might be able to convince them... because it can help you with English, your confidence, and help you build self esteem."

For him, though, the best thing about a book is when it takes him into another world. "If you try to take your head out of it, it makes you think 'oh my god what's going to happen next?'"

The winning book will be announced in February next year at the Young V&A in London. 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books will be given to children who need them most.

articles.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
articles.text:
If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).

It’s no accident that this retrospective crew is in high gear just as Los Angeles, and Hollywood, hit the skids in real life. Runaway production to other states and overseas has been sapping the heartland of the California film industry for decades: from its peak in 1996, feature film activity in the city had dropped by 50% by 2013 – and has further declined since. The cardiac arrest suffered by theatrical box office during Covid and the post-2022 streaming slowdown pushed it deeper into the red zone: 42,000 jobs have been lost over the last two years. With half-empty studio lots, landmark talking shops like Patrick’s Roadhouse dying out and swathes of iconic neighbourhoods ravaged by wildfires, the current fear is that job-stealing AI will further hollow out the city, inducing an irreversible state of digital dereliction.

No wonder returning to the 60s and 70s to soak up the agent chat at the bar at Musso & Frank, or bask in Sharon Tate basking in her own image at the Bruin theater, is comforting. The late middle-aged LA revivalists like Tarantino, David Fincher (who’s taken over directing from Tarantino on Further Mis-Adventures) and Anderson (who also made the similarly LA-besotted Inherent Vice in 2014) were too young to have experienced that era directly. But hitting working age in the 1990s, the final generation to experience Hollywood’s pre-digital imperial phase, they are the ones now memorialising its heyday as a creative powerhouse.

Like today’s AI inflection point, many of the LA revivalist films deal with a moment of transition. Once Upon a Time is caught between the tail end of the stodgy studio system represented by Leonardo DiCaprio’s floundering star Rick Dalton and the New Hollywood noisy neighbours of Roman Polanski and his ilk. And like today’s furore over AI slop supplanting human-led film-making, a strain of panic runs through the new films about the survival of true cinema. “You know what we gotta do? We gotta redefine the form,” says Pitt, playing a silent-film veteran staring down the barrel of the talkies in Babylon. “The man who puts gasoline in your tank goes to the movies – why? Because he feels less alone there. Don’t we owe him more than the same old shit?” Mia Goth’s porn star Maxine Minx, hoping to cross over to “real” movies in 1985 LA, is on the receiving end of a similar pep talk from her director in MaXXXine.

So staring into the abyss of the San Andreas fault and fearing for its soul is nothing new for Hollywood. Often for the current revivalist crew, it’s an elusive woman who crystallises this search for a halcyon authenticity: “This is the girl”, as David Lynch intuited a long time back in Mulholland Drive. In Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, Sharon Tate is the golden-tressed spirit of aspiring LA – and actor Margot Robbie repeated a similar job with her wild-child ingenue in Babylon (with a near-identical scene of watching herself in the cinema). Inherent Vice isn’t specifically about the film industry, but the disappeared Shasta Fay Hepworth leaves behind an incense whiff of the lost idealism of hippy California. Seemingly hunted by serial killer the Night Stalker, Maxine Minx looks destined to become another LA sacrificial woman – until she bucks the trend and saves herself.

But finding “the girl” – or in other words sifting the real from the fake – is no cinch in Los Angeles, the town that made its name intertwining the two. Trudging in the footsteps of Philip Marlowe, Inherent Vice and David Robert Mitchell’s Under the Silver Lake (2018) both feature pseudo-detectives trying to decode this city of signifiers. Also hanging on a missing girl, the latter film stages its own inquest on Angeleno artistic integrity: its arch-conspiracy leads to a mysterious songwriter who devastates Andrew Garfield’s slacker by telling him he manufactured all his favourite rebel alt.culture.

It’s Tarantino, though, who supplies the subtlest take on the twin spooling of representation and reality in Los Angeles. Already Pulp Fiction – the movie he has deemed closest in spirit to Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood – took place at a retro-tinted remove from the actual city. But his 2019 masterpiece lingered in backlots and dressing rooms, making full use of its backstage pass to tease out the interplay of artifice and life in a series of paradoxes. It’s Cliff Booth, the behind-the-scenes stalwart, who supplies the film’s movie-star moment when he walks tall into the Manson family’s Spahn Ranch. Meanwhile, screen star Rick Dalton gets a lower-key, realistic triumph: besting his insecurities and alcoholism to finally deliver “the best acting I’ve ever seen in my whole life”. And in rescuing Sharon Tate from her grisly real-life fate, Tarantino delivers the ultimate movie resurrection.

But perhaps, pained by an industry on the brink, the new pack of sentimentalist LA redeemers wilfully misremember their history. Perhaps the reality is there was no Hollywood golden age, no well of authenticity. Fabrication and artifice are the city’s true trades. Tarantino also knows this, as the irony about movie-star facades – Bruce Lee included – in Once Upon a Time lets on. Paul Thomas Anderson is even clearer about this tawdry fabulation factory in Licorice Pizza, with its San Fernando valley milieu of cocky teen actors, Sean Penn’s leathery star vaingloriously recreating a stunt outside the Tail O’ the Cock restaurant on Ventura Boulevard, and an explosive cameo for legendary hairdresser turned cokehead producer Jon Peters. The most truthful scene in the otherwise coarse and forced Babylon is the one-shot through the multitude of entertainments shooting out on the desert lot: the radical, illusionistic inauthenticity of Hollywood production in full flow. As Cliff Booth has it in Mis-Adventures: “I know better than to get in the way of a good story.”

The least bewitched film about the city is Thom Andersen’s 2003 cine-essay Los Angeles Plays Itself, which is clear-eyed about its penchant for constant self-erasure and reinvention. In this sprawling “any city”, there is no there there – least of all in Hollywood. This floating constellation of studios and production companies is a fungible entity. He points out that Culver City in 1937 almost renamed itself Hollywood, trying to grab some of the glory. Even the sign itself – which, unlike film-industry self-obsession, Andersen tolerates – is testimony to this incorrigible restlessness: “Maybe I find it poignant that a decayed advertisement for a real-estate development could become a civic landmark.”

With AI knocking, Los Angeles and Hollywood are about to head somewhere else. Likely the industry will absorb and integrate the technology, and emerge leaner and meaner, a little more cynical, a little less interesting. Some people will have to find new lines of work. Like Cliff Booth, you could do worse than becoming a fixer. There’s never a shortage of work, because Hollywood, and Los Angeles, can’t be fixed.

articles.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
articles.text:
Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist.

The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing, and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life.

The quality is high this time: Bailey is on fine gadfly form here, hop-skipping from jokes about “the cheesecake Ceaușescu” in the White House to tales of speed awareness courses at the Ramada Inn, Watford. There’s musing on the impact of Shakespeare’s “To be or not to be” when translated into different languages, and visual gags on an upstage screen about what all those Georgian women in Gainsborough paintings may be concealing beneath their skirts.

There’s more: a song with shadow-puppet animation about a big-headed woman and her ferret; all seven deadly sins committed in a kebab shop in 15 seconds flat. In another comic’s hands, this might seem frivolous or unfocused – and occasionally here (his bit about animating Chekhov plays with his belly button fluff, say) the dottiness can feel attenuated. But usually Bailey’s contagious delight in his off-beam interests, and the comic and musical virtuosity applied to them, keep proceedings buoyant. There’s a distinctive pleasure, finally, in enjoying – far from the nearest niche – the popular success of an act that strikes zero compromise with orthodoxy.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack
articles.text:
It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish.

Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits.

Yet this time around the concerns are more modern, and global. Appropriately, given its mock-Florida geography, there are plenty of A-list rap acts including Cardi B, Playboi Carti and Gunna, while songs from Rauw Alejandro, Jhayco and more give a substantial Latin flavour. Even if it’s not quite as region-specific as GTA V’s soundtrack of hip-hop, punk and psychedelia was to southern California, you can still imagine plenty of this material wafting around real-life Miami.

The brand new songs collected on the soundtrack album are only a small fraction of the music heard in Grand Theft Auto VI. Within the game are 22 radio stations, each with a playlist of at least two dozen songs each with its own genre focus, from country to blues to global music and pop hits new and old alike. There are 700 songs spanning nine decades licensed here, reflecting the spirit of exploration the game is meant to inspire.

That breadth makes the game feel fresh and exciting every time you play, and there are moments of gleeful serendipity when a playlist delivers the perfect accompaniment for a clean getaway (Mojabi Ghost by Bad Bunny and Tainy) or a moment of viral cheer (a romantic jetski romp set to Carly Rae Jepsen’s Run Away With Me) or a jaw-dropping surprise (Kamikazi, a funky previously unreleased song from the neo-soul legend D’Angelo.)

Despite the endless variety, Rockstar’s shifting aesthetic sensibilities stand out. With rap not quite as pop-culturally central as it once was, Grand Theft Auto VI looks to the nightclub, heralded by Justice’s score and a clear focus on dance-pop artists: Arca, former Blackpink star Jennie, Fcukers and Rina Sawayama. Rockstar’s bet seems to be that this decade of unrest will keep us searching for escapism on the dancefloor, as well as in their own virtual worlds.

What is certain is the extraordinary cultural clout Grand Theft Auto has amassed, securing true megastars such as Travis Scott, Dua Lipa and Morgan Wallen to record new tracks. That starriness gives a celebratory bent to the album; almost every act seems to sense the scale of the occasion, and strongly delivers. There are a few misfires – regional Mexican music revivalists Fuerza Regida settle for a run-of-the-mill urbano jam – and there aren’t many moments to slow down, though when you need a break from boosting cars and high-stakes stickups, the dreamy, heartbreaking Largate, by Helado Negro and Kali Uchis, is a standout.

Grand Theft Auto is notoriously fond of taking the piss. In-game adverts lambast US gun culture and rightwing politicians; podcasters and TV programmes are routinely mocked. Music, however, is the one place where the games are deadly serious. Last time we were in Vice City, Rockstar seemed content to use music as a mere signifier of the era. Today, it may be the most important non-algorithmic curator of music in the world. It’s heartening that their taste in music is this good – criminally so, you might say.

articles.title: Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave
articles.text:
When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming.

Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla, after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both.

If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. The flipside of this idea, that nature is not just a scenic backdrop to human history but a living participant in it, would have, let’s just say, consequences for German painting after 1945. Here is the challenge that Kiefer has spent his career meeting: how to paint the landscape as an unspoilt refuge from society when it is littered with mass graves?

Given that his forests are haunted by these horrors, it is inevitable that a series of paintings of hunters’ lookouts, displayed back to back on trolley wheels, should call to mind camp watchtowers, their high windows like unblinking eyes. And that an eight-metre-tall canvas of a building’s interior collapsing into a bonfire of real charcoal planks (affixed to the canvas and painted with brilliant licks of flame) should imply more than the destruction of an artist’s inventory. Here is a world of fire and ash, burning so that it might be reborn. The dark glamour, the virtuoso handling of the paint and the sheer scale are seductive.

Yet the power of the studio paintings derives more from their marvellous combination of colours and textures than their symbolism. For a hermetic artist, who magpies from esoteric theories as scattered as alchemy, string theory and Kabbalah in a search for hidden correspondences that can sometimes manifest as a generalised profundity, this focus on a subject qualifies as restraint. I was wondering whether this might even herald a new and (relatively) pared-back late style when I came to a painting of a naked man resembling the artist lying in a blasted landscape, learning from the handout that it was titled (in Latin, no less) On the Third Day He Rose Again, and thought: aha. Faint hope.

It is not surprising that an octogenarian artist’s thoughts should turn to mortality, and everyone must make their own private sense of that approaching horizon. It’s your funeral, as they say. But the enormous paintings that end this show – featuring solitary men staring morosely into pits, lying in open graves, and being miraculously resurrected – link the archetypal figure of the artist to the martyrdom of Christ and the genocides of the 20th century. Even for someone as indifferent to appearing pretentious as Kiefer, this is heady stuff.

In fairness, the idea that the death of the artist might redeem humanity is – I think – intended as bleakly ironic: one man gazing blankly into what could be a mass grave is identified as Narcissus. But at worst, it seems crass. Two paintings in the same room are dedicated to the poets Paul Celan and Ezra Pound. Here it is important to know that Celan, who was Jewish, wrote the line that is quoted in Kiefer’s painting while he was imprisoned in a forced labour camp and his parents were being murdered. Pound, at this time, was living in Italy and broadcasting violently antisemitic propaganda on behalf of the fascists. It is not enough to place them together without context, as if their incorporation into Kiefer’s intricately networked but generally obscure artistic universe constitutes some magical resolution of these tensions.

Kiefer has stated his commitment to “ambivalence”, which I understand to mean that his role as an artist is to memorialise the horrors rather than unravel the contradictions that produced them. But when art reproduces the past rather than processes it, we are bound to get stuck in a loop – and we are now living through another conspiratorial age in which the profusion of myths and alternative belief systems serves to obscure clear truths.

These last paintings seem to me realised on such a vast scale not just because the artist wants to overwhelm the viewer, but because the subjects he has taken on are, in the end, too big for him to manage.

Anselm Kiefer: Des Malers Atelier is at White Cube Bermondsey, London, until 24 January
